name: Activepieces
description: Open-source workflow automation platform (Zapier alternative) with AI agent steps and a built-in MCP server.
scored_configuration: Self-hosted community edition 0.92.0 from docker-compose.yml with tools/deploy.sh and .env.example defaults (AP_EXECUTION_MODE=UNSANDBOXED, unrestricted network mode, telemetry on), scoring a flow's Run Agent step with author-attached piece tools.
headline: An Activepieces agent step runs unattended: every tool the author attaches executes without human approval, using the author's broadly scoped app accounts. If the content it processes (an email, a webhook payload, a web page) carries injected instructions, the agent can leak data through its built-in web fetch and send, post or write on the author's behalf. The tool layer is better than average, with author-pinned fields, credentials kept away from the model and an address-filtered fetch, but there is no way to stop a running step. In the shipped execution mode, pieces and code run in the worker container that holds the key to every stored credential.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: An agent step acts through the connections (stored app accounts) that the flow author attaches to each tool, and the shipped integrations request broad OAuth scopes, for example Gmail send, compose and modify, and wide Slack user scopes. The server keeps an unattended agent run inside its own project: it accepts runs only from a running flow, rejects chat-only and cross-project tools for unattended runs, and refuses to switch projects. Nothing narrows authority per request or per end user: whoever triggers the flow (a webhook caller, an email sender, a chat visitor) gets the author's accounts. A hijacked agent therefore holds full-account access to every connected service.
criteria.notes: D is L0 because shipped credential types default to broad scopes, not because a control is opt-in; G1 does not apply.

S.finding: Each tool uses a dedicated stored connection, but the shipped OAuth credential types request broad read-and-write scopes (Gmail send/compose/modify, Slack user write scopes).
S.gap: Built-in credential types do not request minimal or read-only scopes, so read and write tools share one broad grant.

C.finding: Unattended runs are accepted only from the engine principal, confined to the run's project, and chat-only or cross-project tools are rejected server-side; every configured piece tool resolves its connection inside that project.
C.gap: Authorization is per project, not per requesting principal: anyone who can trigger the flow acts with the author's connections.

B.gap: Credentials are long-lived account-wide grants, not scoped short-lived tokens.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: An agent step in a flow runs unattended and never asks a human before acting: configured piece tools, flow tools and MCP tools execute as soon as the model calls them. The agent code does contain an approval mechanism, but it belongs to the enterprise chat assistant; in a flow step every approval request is automatically declined, and none of the step's own tools ever requests one. Flows can include separate approval steps, but they do not gate the agent's individual tool calls. The actions an agent step can take through its tools, such as sending email or posting messages, are mostly irreversible.
criteria.notes: The enterprise chat assistant (not part of the scored configuration) shows the exact call and matches approved input to executed input; flow-step runs do not use it.

S.finding: No approval condition exists for configured tools in an unattended agent step; the approval wait returns 'declined' for flow-step runs and configured tools never call it.
S.gap: No per-call human approval for any tool in an agent step.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: An agent step only gets the tools its author attached, plus web fetch and search, and the model cannot add tools. For each piece tool the model writes a plain-language instruction and a server-side filler works out typed inputs; fields the author pinned always win, the connection is never chosen by the model, and a custom API call may only target a path on the connection's own API. The built-in web fetch is a read-only GET that blocks private, loopback and cloud-metadata addresses at connection time and bounds size and time, and configured tools are capped at 50 calls per run. Unpinned fields accept any value the model picks (any recipient, any record), MCP tools pass arguments through unchanged, and requests made by pieces themselves are not address-filtered unless the operator turns on the strict network mode.

S.finding: Typed inputs with author-pinned fields that override model values, no model-chosen credential, a host restriction on custom API calls, and an address-filtered fetch tool; unpinned fields are free.
S.gap: Unpinned piece inputs (recipients, targets, amounts) are not checked against allowlists, and pieces' own outbound requests are unfiltered by default.

evidence.contains: must be a path on the connection

C.finding: All configured piece tools go through the shared input filler and its checks; MCP tools pass arguments straight to the remote server.
C.gap: Extension (MCP) tools are not wrapped by a shared validation layer.

D.finding: The step receives only the tools its author attached plus read-only web tools; the model cannot load or enable tools, and chat-only tools are excluded and rejected server-side.
D.gap: The built-in fetch tool is always present, so even a step with no tools has an outbound channel; L4 also needs a stronger S.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: Activepieces runs code steps, and through its built-in MCP server and AI code generation that code can be written by a model. In the shipped configuration (the unsandboxed execution mode) new code steps run in a Deno process that cannot read the filesystem or start programs but has full network access, while older code steps and every piece run as ordinary processes in the worker container. That container runs as root and holds the platform's credential encryption key and database password, so anything that escapes reaches every stored credential; the project's security policy describes this mode as meant for trusted operators. A much stronger mode that runs the engine inside the isolate sandbox and code with no Deno permissions exists but is off by default.

cap.reason: Opt-in mechanism: off in the scored default configuration.

S.finding: The engine runs inside the isolate sandbox under a separate unprivileged uid with a minimal read-only filesystem and process limits, and code steps run in Deno with no permissions.
S.gap: Not kernel-separated (shares the host kernel and network namespace).

C.finding: The whole engine process, including pieces and code steps, starts inside isolate in this mode.
C.gap: No explicit fail-closed guarantee was verified for every spawned process.

D.finding: Off by default: the shipped environment selects the unsandboxed mode.
D.gap: Off by default.

B.finding: The box shares the container's network and the engine still receives the run's decrypted connections.
B.gap: Network egress is not restricted inside the box.

S.finding: New code steps run in a Deno process with file access limited to the step folder and temp, no subprocesses, but network, system info and a filtered environment granted; older code steps and the engine itself run as plain Node child processes.
S.gap: No OS-level isolation in the default mode; the Deno permissions grant unrestricted network.

C.finding: Deno restrictions cover new code steps only; legacy code steps and every piece run in plain processes in the worker container.
C.gap: Piece code and legacy code steps run outside any sandbox.

D.finding: The shipped environment selects the unsandboxed execution mode; the Deno restriction depends on a per-step flag that new steps set.
D.gap: The sandboxed modes are an environment-variable change away and the default mode is the unsandboxed one; no per-call escalation exists.

B.finding: Code runs in the worker container as root, with unrestricted network to internal services; that container's environment holds the platform's credential encryption key, signing secret and database password, so escaping the Deno restriction (or any legacy step) reaches every stored credential.
B.gap: Platform secrets and stored credentials are reachable from the execution environment.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: An agent step is meant to process untrusted content: trigger data such as incoming emails, webhook payloads and chat messages is placed into its prompt, and tool results and fetched web pages flow back into its context. The code marks every flow-step run as having read untrusted data, but nothing acts on that mark in unattended runs, and the tools stay fully available without approval. A hijacked step can therefore read private data through the author's connections and send it out through the built-in web fetch or any write tool, and it can take irreversible actions such as sending email, with no human involved.

cap.reason: B is L0: a hijacked unattended agent step can leak data and take irreversible actions with no human involved.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: An agent step has no memory of its own: each run starts a fresh conversation, the long-term memory tool is limited to the enterprise chat assistant, and there are no instruction files loaded from a workspace. The one persistent source it reads is the knowledge base, which only people can upload to; searches are confined to the run's project and come back as tool results, and an unattended run cannot move to another project. A poisoned knowledge-base file would still be read by every later run in the project with nothing marking it as untrusted, though it can be seen and deleted in the interface.

S.finding: The model has no write path to memory in a flow step; knowledge-base files are uploaded by people and returned as tool results.
S.gap: Knowledge-base content carries no expiry or review step before it is used.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: Pieces, the integrations an agent uses as tools, are npm packages from Activepieces' catalog; the worker installs the exact version a flow names, skips install scripts and only accepts dependency releases older than three days. There is no hash or signature check on what is installed, and remote MCP servers attached to an agent step are used as found, with their tool lists re-read on every run. Pieces are installed automatically when an author picks them, and they run inside the same engine process as the flow, with its decrypted connections and engine token, as root in the worker container in the default mode.

S.finding: Pieces are installed at the pinned version from the curated catalog with install scripts disabled and a minimum release age for dependencies; no integrity check, and MCP tool definitions are not pinned.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: Stored connections are encrypted in the database with an instance key kept in the environment file, and the agent never sees them: the model only writes an instruction, the server attaches the credential when the action runs, and the credential is stripped from inputs echoed back to the model and the run record. Server logs use a redaction list for common secret fields, and the engine process starts with a cleaned environment. Product telemetry to PostHog is on by default; it drops names and emails for self-hosted installs. The connections themselves are long-lived account-wide grants, and the encryption key lives in the same environment file as the rest of the configuration on the worker that runs pieces and code.

S.finding: Credentials are encrypted at rest with an instance key from the environment, substituted only at execution time, and redacted from model-visible and logged inputs; logs use a redaction path list.
S.gap: No OS keychain or secret manager by default: the decryption key sits in the plain environment file.

C.finding: Logs, run records and model-bound inputs are covered and the engine gets a scrubbed environment; tool outputs and debug logs of tool input are not filtered.
C.gap: Tool results and error text are not scanned before reaching the model, logs or the run record.

D.finding: Telemetry is on by default and content-free for self-hosted editions.
D.gap: Telemetry should be opt-in.

B.finding: Leaked connections are long-lived broad OAuth grants; the instance key that decrypts all of them sits in the worker container's environment.
B.gap: Credentials are not scoped or short-lived.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: Each agent step's full conversation, including every tool call with its inputs and outputs, is saved in the database and updated after each step, and the step's result in the flow run lists the tool calls too. Runs are attributed to the project and the flow run, but the requesting person is recorded as the project owner, not whoever triggered the flow. A dedicated agent-action audit event exists, but only the enterprise audit log listens for it. Progress saves are best-effort: failures are retried briefly and then ignored while the agent keeps acting.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: An agent step stops after 20 model steps by default (authors can raise this to at most 1,000), after a per-turn token ceiling, or after two hours, and each tool call times out after five minutes. Configured tools are capped at 50 calls per run, repeated identical failing calls are short-circuited, and a project can start at most 60 agent runs a minute. There is no way to stop a running agent step: the cancel check that the chat assistant polls is not started for flow steps, so only the two-hour backstop ends a runaway run, and flows it called keep running on their own.

S.finding: Step cap, per-turn token ceiling, wall-clock backstop, tool timeouts and a repeated-failure breaker are enforced; flow-step runs have no operator halt.
S.gap: No working stop for flow-step agent runs; cancellation is never polled.

C.finding: Limits apply to the top-level loop and to each tool call; flow tools run as separate flow runs with their own timeout and count only against the 50-call cap.
C.gap: Called flows do not share the agent's time or token budget.

D.finding: Defaults are moderate (20 steps), the model cannot raise them, and the request schema caps the step budget at 1,000; a flow tool can start another agent step with a fresh budget.
D.gap: Delegating to a flow that contains its own agent step starts a fresh step budget.

B.finding: The wall-clock backstop is two hours and nothing can stop a flow-step run before it.
B.gap: Run-time ceiling is hours and stopping is not possible.

critical_findings.summary: Agent tools act with long-lived, broadly scoped OAuth grants (for example Gmail send/modify), so a hijacked agent controls the connected accounts.
In the shipped unsandboxed mode, pieces and code steps run as root in the worker container whose environment holds the credential encryption key and database password.

Untrusted trigger data and tool results reach an unattended agent that holds account access, an arbitrary-URL fetch and write tools with no approval, so a prompt injection can leak data and act irreversibly.
Piece packages run inside the engine process with the flow's decrypted connections, as root in the worker container in the default mode.

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: trigger data placed into the agent prompt (run-agent.ts:140), tool results, ap_fetch_url (web-media-tools.ts:13-26)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: the author's connected accounts with broad OAuth scopes (gmail auth.ts:10-17)
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: arbitrary GET via ap_fetch_url and author-attached write tools, unattended (agent-tool-policy.ts:71-76, configured-tools.ts:127-134)

fixes.summary: Honour stop requests for flow-step agent runs by polling the existing cancel flag, as the chat assistant does.
Once an unattended run has read untrusted content (already tracked), block the fetch tool and require approval for write tools.
Offer per-tool approval for agent steps that shows the exact resolved input to an approver, and turn it on for write actions by default.
Keep the encryption key, signing secret and database password out of the worker container that runs pieces and code, and run it as a non-root user.
Request minimal OAuth scopes per action and let authors attach read-only connections to agent tools.

reaudit_log.reason: The cancel check is only started for non-flow-step sources (execute-agent-run.ts:174-178), so flow-step runs have no cooperative halt.
Unpinned piece inputs are free and piece HTTP requests are not address-filtered in the default unrestricted network mode (system.ts:68); only the built-in fetch tool is filtered.
Knowledge-base isolation is per project (knowledge-base.service.ts:219), not per user as the L3 anchor's L2 base requires.
Encryption at rest uses an instance key from the environment file, not a keychain or secret manager; the L3 anchor's first element is not met.
Flow tools can run flows that contain their own agent step, which starts a new step budget (only the per-project run rate limit bounds this).
